runs.notes: 10Web needs no company data — email, first name, last name, password were enough. The AI first presents a plan that has to be approved before generation starts; that approval step blocked the build until it was clicked. The result is a WordPress site on a 10web.cloud subdomain, and the generated content itself is solid: all three services with prices, a contact section, studio text. But the front page was never assigned, so the shared URL is empty, and the contact form is inert. Both are setup failures a normal user would hit too. Scored against all eight landing criteria after the spec was aligned to the same eight-point scale as the booking tests. Added 2026-11-05: the free trial has since ended. my.10web.io logs in but every website route redirects to /upgrade-plan, and app.10web.io no longer resolves, so the 10web.cloud URL from the run cannot be retrieved. The screenshots in /artifacts remain the only evidence of the published page.

runs.notes: One prompt, one run of the plan, 32 minutes, 8 of 8 — and the first run in this set where the storefront half and the admin half both work in the same build. Bolt wrote a real database table and wired the contact form to it: the message shows up as a row in contact_messages, which is the check that most builders fail. The catalogue is the strongest content in any Bolt run (ten works, dimensions, a paragraph per painting, curated-looking picsum images), and the cart, checkout and reference number all hold. Two honest limits: the order is not stored anywhere server-side, so the confirmation disappears on reload although the brief asked for it to survive; and the site is a client-side app, so all ten works live behind /#/ and only the home page is visible to a crawler. No horizontal scroll at 320, 390 or 430 px, no console errors; axe finds contrast on the small caps labels.

runs.notes: The third build of the day and the quietest: one prompt, 30 minutes, nothing to correct. This is the only landing run where the form both confirms and stores — the message showed up as a row in the project database, which none of the page builders managed. The layout is calm and deliberate (deep green, serif headings, an italic service list) and the copy reads like a studio rather than a template. The caveat is the one that applies to every Bolt run: it is a client-side app, so the address bar stays on / and crawlers see one page, which for a landing page matters less than for a shop. The free daily allowance ran out as this build finished, so the page could not be adjusted afterwards; nothing needed adjusting.

The reading part is the best of any tool here: clean typography, proper headings, and publishing is one switch that produces a public notion.site address in seconds. The interactive part does not exist — no forms, no stored data, no reference numbers. Content was pasted as markdown and Notion turned it into headings, paragraphs and bullet lists without a single fix. The page carries a Notion 'Get started' button in the header and a cookie banner, both injected by the platform.
